newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China oil import tariff cuts may be WTO linked - sources.
newsitem.headline: China oil import tariff cuts may be WTO linked - sources.

text.p: China's sharp cuts in oil product import tariffs have sparked speculation that they may be linked to a bid to speed up its entry into the World Trade Organisation (WTO), industry sources said on Friday.
A number of Asian oil traders, including those from China's state-owned SINOCHEM, told Reuters that China has reduced fuel oil import tariffs to three percent from 12 percent.

Gas oil import tariffs have also been cut to three percent from six percent, they said. However, there has been no change in China's crude oil import tariff of 2.5 percent and the nine percent tariff on gasoline, they said.
Traders in Singapore, Hong Kong and South Korea said they were certain China reduced its oil import tariffs starting November 11.
"Yes, import tariffs for fuel oil has been cut from the previous 12 percent to three percent from (last) Monday," an oil trader in Hong Kong said.
"That is why there were a lot more buyers and also for prompt (end November) supplies," he added.

An oil trader in Singapore said: "There were a lot more enquiries this week for oil imports from China. On Monday, some Chinese importers have cleared their oil cargoes based on the new tariffs at the customs, so it cannot be wrong, it cannot just be rumours."
Officials from China's customs office in Beijing said that the government had not issued any statements announcing the tariff cuts.
China rarely announces oil tariff or price changes publicly.
Oil importers in China said they had heard that Beijing planned to cut import tariffs, but they had not seen any official documents.

Oil markets in Asia have been rife with rumours since early November that China planned to lower its oil import tariffs to gain entry into the WTO. Singapore will host the WTO ministerial meeting during December 9-13.
Beijing has been been pushing to join the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), the WTO's predecessor, since 1987.

However, its entry has been stalled because Beijing wants to join under more lenient rules for developing countries, while the United States has insisted that the Chinese economy was too big for such treatment.
China has also attacked the U.S. for blocking its accession by setting overly stringent requirements for its entry.

On November 14, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, said Washington was not prepared to soften its basic demands that China agree to open up its markets to imports before being allowed in the global organisation.
Oil traders noted that while China has made more enquiries for oil products to be delivered during end-November or December, its actual imports have not risen significantly.
China's monthly gas oil (diesel) imports this year have averaged 500,000 tonnes, while fuel oil imports have averaged about 400,000 tonnes.
Traders said high international spot oil product prices continued to deter Chinese importers.

High sulphur fuel oil prices in the benchmark Singapore market has risen to $120.50 per tonne on November 14 from $116.00 on November 5. Gas oil prices hit a five-year high on Wednesday at $30.80 per barrel.
Traders attributed the increase in fuel oil and gas oil prices to increased regional demand and the recent surge in crude oil prices.
